exercise.title: Sus2, sus4, add9 or plain
exercise.why: A sus chord gives up its 3rd for the 2nd or the 4th and an add9 keeps the 3rd and adds the 2nd on top, so asking whether the 3rd is there and where the new note sits names all four chords.

cells.text:
Press a chord box below to hear the chord. Go from Dsus2 to D to Dsus4 and back: one note climbs from the 2nd to the 3rd to the 4th, and the other two stay.
Keep going until you can tell which of the three is sounding with your eyes closed.

Tap {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} on the staff below: C, the plain chord. Tap {{1}}, the ringed {{2}} and {{5}} for Csus2, then {{1}}, the ringed {{4}} and {{5}} for Csus4.
Then tap {{1}} {{3}} {{5}} again and add the {{2}} from the octave above: Cadd9, with its 3rd still there.

Press a chord box below to hear the chord: the same four chords on C. Then look away, press a box without choosing, and name the chord before you look.
Ask two things: is the 3rd there, and if it is not, did it go down to the 2nd or up to the 4th.
If C and Cadd9 sound alike, press one after the other and listen for the note on top.
